summary.summary: Somerset's year-end treasury report shows borrowing of £716m against a £990m ceiling, with everything compliant — but 39.4% of the debt falls due within twelve months, close to the council's own 50% limit, so a large slice must be refinanced at whatever rates arrive. Housing-account financing costs took 11% of housing income this year and the council's own projections take that to 18.3% by 2030/31. The legacy commercial property portfolio (bought for £301m, written down heavily) is being sold off: £33.3m of sales this year at a £4.7m net gain, £82.3m still to go.
summary.as_of_url: https://somerset.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s66252/Annual Treasury Year End Report 2025-2026 and Appendix 1.pdf

compliance.notes: Strong core treasury strategy: an exemplary Arlingclose-style liability benchmark (charted to 2075 and actively used), thorough counterparty/creditworthiness framework, full indicator suite over six years, and a completed exit review of legacy commercial investments. The weak flank is the commercial/non-treasury disclosure set within the supplied papers - no commercial-income-to-revenue ratio (PI-08), no proportionality demonstration (COM-03) and no service/commercial investment limits (COM-09); much of this should live in the separate Non-Treasury Investment Strategy (Appendix T/E), which was not among the supplied PDFs, and the sterling-only borrowing statement (BOR-03) and specified/non-specified categories (INV-05) are also missing from the TMS itself.

gaps.evidence: TMSS pp.5-6: separate GF (Table 2a) and HRA (Table 2b) debt-vs-CFR trajectories

Budget p.39 para 137: disposal income 'factored into the MTFP in supporting the Council's financial position'; TMSS pp.13-14 paras 52-56 IFRS9 fair-value position of pooled funds (pound 7.041m unrealised loss)

findings.paper_title: Item 10a Appendix A - 2025-26 Q1 outturn September 2026
findings.headline: Investment income fell to 36% of quarterly expectation
findings.detail: Investment income in Q1 2026/27 was £0.697m against a projection of £1.950m, a shortfall of £1.253m. This marks a significant underperformance relative to the quarterly budget.
findings.matters: Weak investment returns worsen the fund's annual deficit and, if sustained, increase pressure for higher employer contributions from the council.
findings.figures: Investment income: £0.697m actual vs £1.950m quarterly projection; annual budget £7.750m

findings.paper_title: Item 10a Appendix A - 2025-26 Q1 outturn September 2026
findings.headline: Retirement lump sums ran £1.8m ahead of quarterly forecast
findings.detail: Lump sum payments on retirement in Q1 reached £5.560m against a quarterly projection of £3.750m, £1.810m above budget. This suggests either more retirements than anticipated or higher benefit entitlements per retiree.
findings.matters: Higher-than-expected retirement activity accelerates the fund's cash depletion and reduces the pool available for investment returns.
findings.figures: Lump sum on retirement: £5.560m actual vs £3.750m projected; annual budget £15.000m

findings.paper_title: Item 10a Appendix A - 2025-26 Q1 outturn September 2026
findings.headline: Transfer values paid far exceeded quarterly budget
findings.detail: Actual transfer values paid in Q1 were £7.674m against a quarterly projection of £3.000m, an adverse variance of £4.674m. This represents more than double the expected member transfers out of the scheme in the quarter.
findings.matters: Unexpected pension member activity could signal scheme changes or member concerns; if sustained, it increases cash outflows and may require higher council contributions to sustain the fund's funding level.
findings.figures: Transfer values paid: £7.674m actual vs £3.000m projected (Q1); full-year budget £12.000m

findings.headline: System migration due to complete 20 July but backlogs persist; resource needs for recovery still being assessed
findings.detail: Final system merge (consolidating four systems into NEC platform) scheduled for 20 July 2026. As of mid-July, backlogs remain and the council was still "looking at what additional resources we need." Consequences include delayed billing, incorrect benefit payments, and loss of Housing Benefit subsidy. Backlog recovery plans developed but resource allocation unclear.
findings.matters: Unresolved backlogs during collection season threaten revenue cash flow; loss of Housing Benefit subsidy is direct financial loss; unclear resource planning signals ongoing operational strain.
findings.figures: Risk RB009 scored 12 (Q2), 16 (Q3), 16 (Q4), 16 (Q1); Inherent and Current scores both 16 (L4 × I4), target 8. System migration completion date 20 July 2026.
findings.quote: Resources have been focused on system migration, which is due to finish on 20 July 2026, at which time we will commence service recovery and backlog clearance... We are looking at what additional resources we need to deal with the backlog of work.

findings.headline: New risk: pay uncompetitiveness preventing recruitment post-restructure; vacancies only partially filled
findings.detail: New risk RB015 (added 15 July 2026) identifies that Somerset Council salaries are perceived as uncompetitive compared to alternative employers, preventing recruitment in Revenues and Welfare. Post-restructure vacancies have "only been partially filled through an initial round of recruitment." Further recruitment is planned but not yet complete.
findings.matters: Inability to compete on pay signals underlying budget constraints and indicates service capacity will remain constrained until positions are filled.
findings.figures: Risk RB015 scored 16 in Q1, target 8; marked NEW, added 15 July 2026; vacancies "only been partially filled through an initial round of recruitment"
findings.quote: Comparative salaries are seen to be higher than being offered by Somerset Council
